name: Roofing
seoDesc: Roofing: work out house base area from the house length and the house width. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Roofing calculator turns the house length, the house width and more into house base area. Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The results leave the screen the moment you edit a field; press Calculate and they come back updated, so a single changed input shows its own effect.

sections.title: How does the Roofing calculator work?
sections.html:
The Roofing calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports house base area in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the house length, the house width, the roof pitch and the unit price.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Roofing calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

House base area=house length × house width
Roof pitch (%)=the tangent of (roof pitch)
Roof pitch (x:12)=12 × roof pitch (%)
Roof area=house base area ÷ the cosine of (roof pitch)
Roof area=total cost ÷ unit price

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.html:

  • Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • %, opening in percent
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Roofing calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the house length, the house width and the roof pitch — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Roofing calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns house base area, derived from the house length, the house width and the roof pitch. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Roofing calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the house length, the house width, the roof pitch and the unit price, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter house length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. House length opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Roofing calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
